crumbs.name: AI Adoption and Governance in Life Sciences

reading.body:
Training is the part of AI adoption that successful programmes invest in most, and in the EU it is now a legal obligation, not a choice.

The pattern here is that workforce capability is treated as infrastructure rather than an afterthought. Moderna built an AI Academy with Carnegie Mellon and Coursera and trained more than 2,000 employees. That is a deliberate build, with outside partners, at a scale that reaches well past a pilot group. The EU AI Act now requires providers and deployers to ensure staff have sufficient AI literacy, with that obligation applicable from 2 February 2025. Training tied to real tasks in each role, and recorded, doubles as compliance evidence.

This matters for AI specifically because models and compute deliver nothing on their own. A drugmaker can buy the same frontier models and cloud capacity as its competitors. What it cannot buy off the shelf is a workforce that knows where to apply them. The training layer is where adoption either spreads through an organisation or stalls in a handful of teams.

The data does not say whether Moderna's programme changed research or development outcomes, and it gives no cost, completion rate, or comparison against other drugmakers. It covers one company's programme and one regulation. It says nothing about how training interacts with compute supply or data centre capacity, and nothing here should be read as evidence about that link.
